title: The Secret of Roman Concrete
context:
The Pantheon in Rome, completed in the second century, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its survival is remarkable when set against modern experience. Structures built with contemporary concrete often need major repairs after fifty years, and few are expected to last beyond a century. Even more puzzling are the Roman harbours, built by pouring concrete into seawater, a setting that chemists would expect to damage the material within a few decades. Yet many of these walls and piers remain standing two thousand years later.

For a long time, scholars assumed that the secret lay in the volcanic ash which Roman builders mixed with lime. The architect Vitruvius praised the ash from the region near Naples, and laboratory work confirmed that it reacts with lime and water to form a binder stronger than lime alone. This explanation, however, covers only part of the problem. It tells us why Roman concrete was good when it was new, but not why samples from harbour walls appear to have grown stronger with age.

A research team that drilled cores from an ancient harbour structure found a clue in the pores of the concrete. Crystals of two rare minerals, tobermorite and phillipsite, had grown there slowly over the centuries. Seawater seeping through the material had reacted with the volcanic ash and with the lime, and the new crystals had gradually filled spaces and sealed fine cracks. In other words, the very agent that threatens modern concrete had helped to reinforce the Roman version. The finding suggested that the ancient builders, whether by luck or experience, had created a material that responded to its environment.

A second discovery concerns the small white lumps of lime that are visible throughout Roman concrete. Archaeologists had long interpreted these lumps as signs of careless mixing. A more recent study proposes that they are intentional. According to this view, the builders mixed the ingredients while using quicklime, which is lime that has not yet been combined with water, so that the mixture became extremely hot and produced reactive lumps. When a crack later opened and water entered, the lumps dissolved and then hardened again as a mineral that filled the gap. To test the idea, researchers made concrete using the supposed Roman method and deliberately cracked it. Within two weeks, the cracks had closed, while those in a control sample made by a modern recipe remained open.

Such results should be treated with caution. Roman concrete had weaknesses that engineers cannot ignore: it set slowly, it was weak when pulled or bent, and it could not be combined with steel bars, which are essential for tall buildings and long bridges. There is also a problem of selection. The structures that have survived to the present are the ones that were well made, whereas countless Roman buildings collapsed or were demolished and left no trace. The remarkable durability of the Pantheon may therefore say more about the best builders than about the average one.

Nevertheless, the research has practical value. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, so a material that repaired itself and lasted for centuries would reduce the demand for replacement. Most researchers do not propose copying the Roman recipe exactly. Instead, they hope to borrow selected features, such as the use of reactive lumps for self-repair, and adapt them for modern construction. If they succeed, the ancient builders' most useful legacy may turn out to be not their monuments, but their method.
